My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I would have assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely somewhere in the low-to-mid 600s for the underlying asset. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 605.5 essentially anchors near the current price with only a slight directional lean, reflecting the low expected movement over a single trading session and the assumption that near-term momentum or overnight sentiment was mildly positive. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 608, acknowledging that while short-term trends can persist, the incremental upward drift over five trading days is modest and uncertain. At the one-month horizon, the 615 estimate reflects a continuation of a gentle bullish bias, consistent with a baseline assumption of positive drift in equity or equity-like assets over time, but the conviction behind that specific number is considerably lower than at shorter horizons.

The confidence interval widths were deliberately calibrated to widen with time, reflecting the fundamental principle that uncertainty compounds as the forecast horizon extends. At one day, a range of roughly 33 points (589 to 622) reflects typical intraday-to-overnight volatility and the relatively tight distribution of outcomes over a short window. At one week, the interval expands to 60 points (578 to 638), capturing the possibility of a meaningful trending move or a sharp reversal driven by macro data releases or earnings news. At one month, the 120-point range (555 to 675) acknowledges that a wide variety of macro, geopolitical, and sentiment-driven scenarios could plausibly materialize over four to five weeks.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include unexpected central bank policy shifts, such as a surprise rate decision or hawkish commentary that triggers a sharp repricing of risk assets. A sudden deterioration in credit conditions, a geopolitical shock, or a major earnings miss from a systemically important company could all drive prices well below the lower bounds. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data print, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above the upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where tail events have more time to materialize.

It is also worth noting that my intervals, while wide by short-horizon standards, may still understate true tail risk. Black swan events — sudden liquidity crises, regulatory shocks, or unexpected geopolitical escalations — are structurally difficult to incorporate into symmetric confidence intervals. Real-world return distributions tend to exhibit fat tails, meaning extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest.
